text.t: Green fluorescent protein folds into a barrel of 11 strands, like a tin can.
It comes from a jellyfish that lives in the cold waters of the north Pacific.
Right in the middle of the can sits the chromophore, the part that absorbs light and glows green.
The protein around it shields it from water molecules that would otherwise steal its energy.
The chromophore forms by itself from three amino acids in the chain, here threonine 65, tyrosine 66 and glycine 67.
The file shows them as one fused group, joined to phenylalanine 64 on one side and valine 68 on the other.
One stretch of the chain runs straight through the centre of the can, and the chromophore forms from that central helix.
Threonine 203 sits next to the chromophore.
Changing it to tyrosine or histidine shifts the light toward red, one way scientists made new colours.

does.t: In the jellyfish, GFP takes blue light from another protein, aequorin, and turns it into green light.
Shine ultraviolet light on GFP and it glows bright green.
Scientists attach GFP to other proteins or viruses so they can watch them move inside living cells.

shape.t: Most light-handling proteins need a special molecule added, but GFP builds its own chromophore using only amino acids.
The chromophore needs the folded protein to form and to glow, and oxygen from the surroundings finishes it.
Because it makes its own glow, a cell only needs the gene for GFP to start shining.

text.t: GFP comes from light-making cells of the jellyfish Aequorea victoria.
Scientists have added it to mice, frogs, flies, worms and many other living things.

history.who: M. Ormo, A.B. Cubitt, K. Kallio, L.A. Gross, R.Y. Tsien and S.J. Remington

text.t: This X-ray structure of a GFP with threonine at position 65 was solved at 1.9 angstroms.
It revealed the 11-strand barrel and showed how one change near the chromophore shifts the colour.

compare.t: GFP measures about 5.3 nm from end to end.
That is a little bigger than lysozyme in this gallery, which measures about 4.9 nm.

text.t: The glowing group, made from three amino acids of the chain.
Changing this amino acid shifts GFP's colour toward red.
